Swing

Walking bass, the ride cymbal and syncopated comping

Open the Swing style in the Backing Track

What it is

The rhythm section of small-group jazz from the late 1930s onward: a bass that plays a note on every beat, a drummer whose main voice is the ride cymbal (ding, ding-a, ding, ding-a) with the hi-hat closing on 2 and 4, and a piano or guitar that “comps” (accompanies, complements): short chords placed off the beat, answering the soloist instead of marking time.

A little history

In the 1920s the bass part of a jazz band was usually a tuba or a slapped string bass playing on beats 1 and 3 (the two-beat feel; see Jazz ballad). In the Count Basie band of the mid-1930s, bassist Walter Page walked four even beats a bar, guitarist Freddie Green strummed a quiet chord on every beat, and drummer Jo Jones moved the time-keeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat. Basie himself played sparse fills instead of a full stride left hand. That “All-American Rhythm Section” is where the modern swing feel comes from.

In the 1940s bebop drummers (Kenny Clarke, then Max Roach) moved the pulse to the ride cymbal and used the snare and bass drum for accents (“dropping bombs”). Pianists such as Bud Powell stopped playing on every beat and comped in short syncopated stabs. By the late 1950s, rootless left-hand voicings (Bill Evans, Wynton Kelly, Red Garland) became the standard piano sound: the bassist has the root, so the pianist plays the 3rd, 7th and colour tones. That is the sound the band’s piano uses here.

The band’s version

  • Bass: Walking: root on beat 1, chord tones and scale steps, an approach note on beat 4.
  • Comping: syncopated rhythms chosen from a set of figures (the Charleston, anticipations, and so on).
  • Drums: ride-cymbal pattern, hi-hat on 2 and 4, light comping on the snare.
  • Voicings: rootless piano voicings, shell voicings on guitar. Players add unmarked 9ths and 13ths.

Real walking lines move far more freely than any rule set; the band’s bassist is a beginner’s model.

Listening

Recording Year Listen for
Count Basie Orchestra, One O’Clock Jump 1937 Walter Page’s four-to-the-bar bass, Freddie Green’s guitar, Jo Jones on hi-hat.
Count Basie, Lester Leaps In (Kansas City Seven) 1939 The same rhythm section in a small group behind Lester Young.
Miles Davis Quintet, Oleo (Relaxin’) 1956 Paul Chambers walking, Philly Joe Jones on the ride, Red Garland’s comping.
Miles Davis, Freddie Freeloader (Kind of Blue) 1959 A jazz blues; Wynton Kelly’s comping behind the horns.
Oscar Peterson Trio, C Jam Blues (Night Train) 1962 Ray Brown’s walking bass at its most driving.

More recent

Recording Year Listen for
Tony Bennett & Lady Gaga, Anything Goes (Cheek to Cheek) 2014 A small group walking and swinging behind two singers.
Jon Batiste, I Need You (We Are) 2021 Swing-era rhythm in a Grammy-winning pop record.

Sources

  • Gunther Schuller, The Swing Era (Oxford, 1989), on the Basie rhythm section.
  • Paul Berliner, Thinking in Jazz (Chicago, 1994), chapters on the rhythm section and comping.
  • Mark Levine, The Jazz Piano Book (Sher, 1989), on rootless voicings.
